articles.author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
articles.description:
Royal tour of Caribbean comes as Commonwealth nations renew calls for Britain to engage in reparation talks
King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.
The king arrived in the Bahamas to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit

articles.author: Pippa Crerar and Heather Stewart
articles.description:
Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferred
John Healey has acknowledged the UK faces a “difficult moment” but insisted he would put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget on Wednesday against a turbulent global economic backdrop.
But despite the international uncertainty, the chancellor will signal “fresh hope for the future” as he attempts to sound a more optimistic note, by providing households with breathing space from rising cost of living pressures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
Three-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research finds
AI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.
Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Mark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assault
A former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.
A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Former Met officer who worked with Wayne Couzens found guilty of rape

articles.author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
articles.description:
Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with overpayments will still have to pay
“On the surface it sounds really positive – and I really hope that it is,” says unpaid carer Guy Shahar of the government’s decision to abolish the notorious carer’s allowance cliff edge.
But Shahar is angry that most carers hit with unjust overpayments in the past will still have to repay them, for all the promise of a different future. And he notes that the cliff edge remains in place for four more years, potentially catching out more carers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Change to carer’s allowance cliff-edge rule is not enough, victims say

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told
A group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with petrol to Fairford RAF base by a handler known as Ali, who police believe was working on behalf of Iran, a court heard on Tuesday.
One of the five men tasked with driving to the base called police in the early hours of 27 September after the handler warned the group about a bomb in the vans, prosecutors told Westminster magistrates court.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: RAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’

articles.author: Kiran Stacey and Pippa Crerar
articles.description:
Emissions from exported oil would not count against carbon budget, insiders say – reasoning likely to draw dismay from climate campaigners
The giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.
The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders

articles.author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
articles.description:
Michal Stasiak and Kinga Wydrzynska pleaded not guilty to 11 counts relating to  death of 13-month-old Isabella Stasiak
A 13-month-old girl was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of her parents before she was fatally injured by her mother, a court has heard.
Michal Stasiak, 28, and Kinga Wydrzynska, 26, appeared at Warwick crown court on Tuesday, where they pleaded not guilty to 11 counts related to the death of Isabella Stasiak.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parents inflicted fatal physical and sexual abuse on their baby, Warwick court hears

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Comedian accused of sexual offences against six women said consensual encounters were ‘unfavourably reframed decades later’
Russell Brand told police he had led a “very promiscuous” life and consensual sexual encounters had been “unfavourably reframed decades later”, his trial has heard.
The 51-year-old comedian blamed the allegations on “defamatory and fictitious” media reports. He said in a statement that he had had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios and kissed hundreds of people in public while trying to be “friendly, consensual and warm”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand told police he led a ‘very promiscuous’ life, trial hears

articles.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
articles.description:
From tackling the youth jobs crisis to repairing Brexit’s economic damage, John Healey has his work cut out for him

You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

John Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in the Middle East.
Against a febrile backdrop in global markets, the chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to the fiscal rules.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.description:
Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.
In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.
John Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are b…
articles.title: Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Retailers also report jump in purchases of wind-up radios and torches to deal with extreme weather and cyber-attacks
Sales of tinned foods, bottled water, wind-up radios and torches have surged after the UK government advised households to prepare for emergencies.
Retailers have reported a jump in sales of items linked to preparation for emergencies such as extreme weather or cyber-attacks. The Be Ready campaign was launched last week with the aim of persuading households to lay in supplies to last 72 hours.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile advice

articles.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Student supporters of Reform UK at Oxford college have organised evening with Nathan Cofnas discussing DEI
The University of Oxford’s Oriel College has been urged to cancel an event featuring Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas that has been organised by student supporters of Reform UK.
Arday, 41, was found dead in August after resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship. He had faced intense media scrutiny after Cofnas made unproven accusations of plagiarism against him and said there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser

articles.author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
articles.description:
Home Office refused entry to Judith Clark, 77, invited by RSC to speak about restorative justice after her time in prison
Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour.
Judith Clark, 77, was the inspiration for Walter’s portrayal of prisoners in the Donmar Warehouse all-female Shakespeare trilogy, including Brutus in Julius Caesar and Prospero in The Tempest.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Shabana Mahmood urged to grant visa to former Weather Underground activist

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
Misogyny prevention fund to help tackle sexism at work, school and in public places across UK
The chancellor will give £15m to a dedicated fund to tackle misogyny in workplaces, schools and public places amid concerns in government about the rise of “manosphere” influencers.
The women and equalities minister, Bridget Phillipson, will helm the UK-wide fund, announced last month, marking the first time there has been specific national cash to address misogyny.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concerns

articles.author: Aletha Adu Political correspondent
articles.description:
From ‘everyday fixes’, party management and communications to long-term plans for care and pensions, the PM’s six key acts so far
Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street promising to transform the way Britain works, restore hope and bring an end to years of political division. One hundred days later, the prime minister has announced a series of measures aimed at making everyday life easier, he’s reopened the debate over Britain’s relationship with the EU and set out plans to overhaul public services. He has also managed to maintain an unusually visible public profile, appearing regularly on social media and even taking part in a charity edition of Channel 4’s Gogglebox. Burnham has said he’s been surprised by the public’s appetite for change, insisting his first budget on Wednesday would offer some breathing space for households and businesses.
But the early weeks of his premiership have also exposed tensions between immediate political wins and the structural changes he has promised. Here is how his first 100 days have unfolded in six key ways.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power?

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
Boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £9,000 for sustainable alternatives, expected to be slashed in budget
When Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical about whether the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said.
“I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
articles.description:
As John Healey’s budget decision looms, lender reports 32% rise in profits
A top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK over tax increases expected to be announced in Wednesday’s budget.
HSBC’s chief financial officer, Pam Kaur, said there was “no pressure”, particularly from shareholders in its cornerstone Hong Kong market, to shift out of London despite lobbyists warning higher tax bills could drive big banks’ business abroad.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: HSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxes

articles.author: Phillip Inman Senior economics writer
articles.description:
British Retail Consortium says ‘dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs’ being kept from consumers
Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
Industrial action by senior doctors to begin on 25 November with only emergency cover provided, BMA says
England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their pay and hours, prompting NHS bosses to warn that patients will suffer “pain, discomfort and inconvenience”.
Consultant doctors, who earn an average of £152,000 a year inclusive of overtime and merit awards, will stage a two-day walkout on 25 and 26 November, as hospitals gear up for the extra pressures winter brings.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton
Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question.
Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The regime change we need for Thames Water | Letters

articles.author: Matthew Weaver
articles.description:
London sites to remain open as Prospect and PCS agree to ‘Acas-facilitated talks’ with museum management
A planned strike at the V&A over half-term has been suspended after an improved offer from its management.
Museum staff who were members of the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions had voted to strike on Thursday and Friday in a dispute over pay and working conditions including inadequate toilet and hydration breaks. The strike would have closed the V&A’s main galleries in south Kensington, as well as V&A East, V&A Storehouse and Young V&A in east London.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Unions suspend planned V&A strike after improved pay offer

articles.author: Hilary Osborne
articles.description:
Retirees will get a personal allowance aligned with the new state pension, but experts say it could get complicated
Retirees in the UK on low incomes are expected to be given a new personal allowance so that they do not have to hand any of their state pension to HMRC.
The full details are due to be revealed by the chancellor, John Healey, in Wednesday’s budget, but here is what we know so far.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Healey is expected to shield low-income pensioners from income tax – but how will it work?

articles.author: Press Association
articles.description:
R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023
The R&B singer Chris Brown has been given a suspended sentence after striking a man twice in the head with a tequila bottle in a central London club.
Brown, 37, admitted affray earlier this year after attacking a former friend with a “heavy” tequila bottle on the dancefloor at the Tape private members’ club in Mayfair in February 2023.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London club

articles.author: Sarah Butler and Gwyn Topham
articles.description:
A stretch of London’s Oxford Street is to be vehicle-free as part of £150m government-backed scheme
Much of Britain’s most famous shopping street will be closed to traffic from Monday as the long-awaited pedestrianisation of London’s Oxford Street begins.
About half of the 1.2 mile street will initially be vehicle-free, after decades of planning and dispute over how to best use the street, an important transport thoroughfare and the home for flagship stores for big shopping chains.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How will pedestrianisation of UK’s most famous shopping street work in practice?

articles.author: Rachel Hall
articles.description:
Monzo says 55% of cardholders’ British Museum payments in first hour of latest ticket release were by people under 35
A 1,000-year-old embroidery may be an unusual candidate for a pop culture moment, but young people are seemingly more willing to shell out for tickets for the Bayeux tapestry than spend money on Hollywood blockbusters.
In the first hour that the second round of tickets to view the tapestry were available last Wednesday, payments from Monzo cardholders to the British Museum reached £14,100 and were 48 times that of a normal Wednesday morning. More than half (55%) of those buyers were aged under 35.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top films

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Josh Halliday; produced by Tom Glasser, Scarlet Pestell, Claudia Efemini and Ross Burns; executive producer Sami Kent
articles.description:
After the prime minister recently intervened to defend Manchester City’s beleaguered ownership, many began to ask: just how deep are the ties between Andy Burnham and the UAE? With North of England editor Josh Halliday. Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com
Why did Andy Burnham recently intervene to defend Manchester City’s beleaguered Abu Dhabi owners, days after they were found guilty of one of the biggest cheating scandals in British sporting history?
Today in Focus presenter and city resident Helen Pidd walks through modern Manchester – where Burnham was mayor for nearly a decade – and charts its transformation wrought by Emirati money.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Abu Dhabi bought Andy Burnham’s Manchester - podcast

articles.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
articles.description:
Chancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the media

You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

The public has been told repeatedly that John Healey is so concerned about budget leaks that he has set up defence-style “compartmentalisation” to prevent the Treasury’s financial secrets escaping.
The macho military analogies began in mid-August when Healey was said by the Telegraph to be “on a war footing” to stop the drip of information that he believed had beleaguered Rachel Reeves.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Has Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets?

articles.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: People from marginalised groups more likely to be diagnosed via urgent referral or in emergency setting, research finds 
People from minority ethnic backgrounds in England are up to a third less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via routine screening, and are more likely to be diagnosed in an emergency setting, analysis has found.
The research, carried out by academics at the University of Surrey and funded by the charity Breast Cancer Now, involved analysis of 86,564 adults diagnosed with the disease between 2009 and 2019, from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and the Cancer Registration Tumour and Treatment datasets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Teesside town has come out worst in children’s commissioner’s report, but residents say such rankings are demoralising and counterproductive
“It’s disappointing, it’s just another kicking,” said a youth worker after the town in which they work was labelled as the hardest place in which to be a child in England.
“It suggests our children are living unhappy lives,” said a teacher, who described her pupils as joyful.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Why would I leave?’: Middlesbrough pushes back against ‘hardest place to grow up’ label

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith; the executive producers are Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale
articles.description:
Are we doomscrolling our way into a democratic crisis? That’s what the playwright James Graham fears may be happening, as he suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future
Watch the full episode with James Graham here.
INK, based on James Graham’s stage play, will be released in UK cinemas on 8 January 2027.
Dear England: about the country’s football team under manager Gareth Southgate.
Sherwood (mentioned in the conversation): set in the village where James grew up in the shadow of the miners’ strike.
Quiz: documenting a notorious scandal on the British gameshow Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Culture is stagnant, so politics is stuck’ – playwright James Graham | Radical Thinking – podcast

articles.author: Rachel Hall
articles.description:
Reality TV show returns to focus on childbirth, diversity and the sharing of stories in a social media age
When One Born Every Minute first aired in 2010, viewers loved its fly-on-the-wall take on life in a maternity unit, from midwives idly chatting about unusual pregnancy cravings to parents squabbling over whether to call their child Zeus.
Almost two decades later, as the show is rebooted for a generation who spend their lives on social media, much has changed. Parents now share far more about their struggles with miscarriages, infertility and mental health; audiences have to be lured away from watching reels on their phones with more rigorous storytelling.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I can’t believe I get to see that’: One Born Every Minute is back for a 12th series

articles.author: Michael Goodier
articles.description:
Sewage samples and crime statistics paint a picture of established users taking more cocaine, more often

Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges

Pubs, festivals and workplaces: how cocaine has become an everyday habit

From pub toilets and private parties to football terraces and far-right marches, cocaine has become a familiar presence across modern Britain. Deaths linked to the drug have risen to record levels, while its supply supports a multibillion-pound criminal industry.
But who is using the drug, and how has the picture changed? The figures do not necessarily show millions of new users, but highlight an established market in which some people take more cocaine, more often – and face greater harm as they grow older.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s multibillion-pound cocaine habit

articles.author: Press Association
articles.description:
Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday
Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts of the UK.
Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain

articles.author: Priya Bharadia
articles.description:
Second named storm will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen
The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.
Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Storm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UK

articles.author: Tara Conlan
articles.description:
BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
The David Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.
Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom

Are we doomscrolling our way into a democratic crisis? That’s what the playwright James Graham fears may be happening, as he suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future

articles.title: “Culture is stagnant, so politics is stuck” – playwright James Graham | Radical Thinking – podcast

articles.author: Mark Sweney
articles.description:
World’s second largest brewer says use of drugs such as Wegovy can reduce desire to drink alcohol
Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.
The world’s second-largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month that said the use of GLP-1 medication – such as Ozempic and Wegovy – could reduce the desire to drink alcohol. This in turn could result in “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars, it added.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Boom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubs

articles.author: Presented by Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping, produced by Danielle Stephens, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
The government has given the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield, but that was the easy part. The next big headache is the Rosebank oilfield. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has indicated she might reject this licence because of the project’s expected environmental impact, but could Andy Burnham overrule her to help the chancellor, John Healey?
You can read Kiran Stacey’s exclusive report on Rosebank here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rosebank row: will Labour block the oilfield? – podcast

articles.author: Esther Addley
articles.description:
Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It should never be forgotten’: families recount care home victims’ experiences in wake of Covid findings

articles.description:
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, thanked the prime minister for backing Jackdaw after the Tories approved it in 2022. But Burnham said he made a decision on something the Tories messed up, and the government had made a bridge to the future and the transition to clean energy


UK politics live – latest updates

UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea

Climate campaigners condemn ‘maddening’ decision to approve Jackdaw gasfield

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Andy Burnham says decision on Jackdaw is something the Tories 'messed up' - video

articles.author: Aisha Down
articles.description:
Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say
It happened again. A power outage hit a datacentre in London, and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app.
The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers

articles.description:
Amateur wildlife photographer Rhys Morgan has caught extraordinary footage of one of the largest whale species on Earth. 

While sailing off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales, Morgan and his friends spotted the blowholes of a fin whale in the distance, recognisable by the hooked fin near its tail, a dark grey upper body, white belly, and an asymmetrical jaw that is dark on the left and white on the right.

People who have enjoyed the video online are trying to raise awareness of fin whales being hunted in Iceland and calling on government ministers to take action
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Whale in Wales: amateur photographer captures stunning footage - video

articles.author: Olivia Mansfield
articles.description:
People share their opinions of Andy Burnham's crackdown on 'headphone dodgers' who play loud music on public transport. The prime minister unveiled a campaign against nuisance behaviour on Monday, alongside guidance allowing local transport authorities to levy fines of up to £100 for non-compliance

Andy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport

 Continue reading...
articles.title: British people react to Burnham's campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport – video

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments
On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.
But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off

articles.author: Blake Montgomery
articles.description:
The AI industry is still defined by a careening intensity that’s taking the world’s finances along for the ride

This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here.

Today in tech, we’re discussing Anthropic’s astronomic growth, how a settlement over social media safety dented Meta’s revenue, and Lula’s accusations of interference against Meta.
‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes
Elizabeth Holmes is back in the spotlight: why can’t we look away?
Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US
The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle
Meta plans $95bn stock offering to help cover AI expansion
iPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handset
Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts
Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company
‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anthropic accelerates – for the rest of us, the speed of growth spells precarity

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster
Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.
Having criticised the hit movie in the summer, the tycoon said he would use Grok Imagine to make a “historically accurate” adaptation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film

articles.author: George Chidi
articles.description:
Social media companies including Meta have pulled back on efforts to protect voters from election-meddling lies
Social media feeds are awash with an unprecedented flood of AI-driven disinformation ahead of November’s US midterm elections, according to experts, who warn many posts are probably “slipping through the cracks”.
As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI-driven disinformation running rampant on social media before US midterms, experts warn

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.description:
Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Tis almost All Hallows’ Eve and naturally, the thoughts of all good video game players are turning to horror. 2026 has already been a bloody good year for the genre with Resident Evil Requiem and Silent Hill: Townfall leading the rabble. But this autumn sees a festering surge of indie horror releases, featuring everything from cursed card games to Nazi-hunting penguins. Here are eight terrifying titles we think you should sample while jack-o-lanterns burn and spirits walk the moonlit streets.
Allogloom (PC)
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

articles.author: Jenna Zaza
articles.description:
From apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attention

Gen Z voters: tell us what is guiding your vote in the US midterm elections?

Nelissa Moukoudi, 19, a university student in Canada, noticed a shift once she joined Instagram and TikTok.
“My social life completely plummeted and it felt like my life was only [using] social media and school,” she said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘My social life completely plummeted’: gen Z is fighting back against big tech

articles.author: Sarah Matthews
articles.description:
With six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devices
• The best LED face masks
CurrentBody’s LED masks have long been my favourite. They’re comfortable, simple to use and effective. My previous favourite, the now-discontinued CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask, offered five treatments that used different light wavelengths to address multiple skin concerns. The company’s latest mask, the new Series 3, has the most detailed customisable treatments I’ve ever seen.
This isn’t the first LED mask I’ve tried that allows its user to select different treatments for different areas of the face. The Lustre Renew Pro Facewear allows you to choose from two treatments across four different zones, with 16 possible combinations. The Series 3 takes this much further, allowing you to choose between six light wavelengths across 125 light points on the mask. If you stick to one wavelength per light point, that’s 6125 combinations available. That number is longer than I can reasonably comprehend, so allow me to call its level of customisation endless.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: CurrentBody Series 3 review: a fully customisable LED mask that helps exactly where you need it

articles.author: Aisha Down Global technology reporter
articles.description:
Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans
The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found.
The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groups

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards
Anthropic has filed to go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business.
The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing

articles.author: Amy Hawkins in Beijing
articles.description:
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group 
AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.
Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Graeme Wearden
articles.description:
Tech firm announces two-part fundraising after Elon Musk warns hundreds of AI startups face collapse
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta has announced plans for $95bn (£71bn) of fundraising to cover its AI expenditure, even as Elon Musk warned that funding for smaller players in the sector was drying up.
The owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is a leading investor in AI and is ploughing multibillion-dollar sums into datacentres, the central nervous systems of the technology.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Meta plans $95bn stock offering to help cover AI expansion

articles.author: Gaya Gupta
articles.description:
Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports
Microsoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the latest example of how AI is reshaping tech companies and the greater workforce.
This is the latest of several trimmings Microsoft has made to its workforce this year. The company announced in April that it was offering voluntary retirement to about 7% of its US workforce, which consisted of about 125,000 employees at the time. Its global workforce is made up of about 223,000 workers globally.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts

articles.author: Blake Montgomery and Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.
Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry

articles.author: Oliver Milman
articles.description:
Company imitates reflection of sun from mirrors, prompting pushback from some scientists, environmentalists and California locals
Locals in a rural area of California were recently startled to see dazzlingly bright light shining down from nearby mountains at night, illuminating a swathe of the desert below.
Unbeknown to them, the strange nocturnal illumination was the latest step in a company’s plan to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight on to the Earth during night-time.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism

articles.author: Ima Caldwell
articles.description:
Actor’s storylines in the famous soap will be recut into vertical micro-episodes to be watched on phones – but her fellow cast members say they haven’t been consulted
The long-running Australian soap opera Neighbours is being recut with AI into a microdrama designed to be watched on phones, sparking a debate among the show’s actors and the industry over the wider implications of television archives being mined for new content.
RoseBerry Media, which specialises in making “vertical television” for phones, has repurposed original episodes of Neighbours for distribution on its Epis platform, using an AI-assisted production tool called RedSnapper.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Neighbours is being recut into a microdrama focused on Margot Robbie – and her co-stars aren’t happy

articles.author: Ellie Gibson
articles.description:
We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments
Happy birthday, Lara! This month marks 30 years since Ms Croft first swan-dived into our lives with her unique blend of athletic prowess, archaeological expertise and giant knockers. More than 100 million Tomb Raider games have been sold since. We all remember the good times: the bold design and sheer playability of the original titles; the establishment of Lara as a 90s icon, embodying both lads’ mag culture and girl power; the way she made games cool, even appearing on the cover of the Face. We’ve had blockbuster movies, big budget reboots, and shiny reissues. And who could forget the time we got to powerwash her house?
But no one gets to 30 without a few skeletons in the closet – or in Lara’s case, butlers in the freezer. So here’s a look at the darker parts of her past.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

articles.author: Hilary Osborne
articles.description:
‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accounts
You’ve had a busy morning of life admin, logging into various accounts to check balances and make payments. At the end of a productive few hours you close your laptop and move on to your next job.
What you don’t know is that fraudsters have hijacked your session with the bank and are now able to access your account. You are the victim of cookie theft, which belongs to a type of fraud known as “session hijacking”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts

articles.author: Lucy James
articles.description:
The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Earlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today.
It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to a leaked trailer, was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A farewell to BioWare, maker of some of the best games of the 21st century | Lucy James

articles.author: Nick Romeo
articles.description:
An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude
In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.
“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI
As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.
That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model.
Case size: 49 x 44mm
Case thickness: 12mm
Weight: 63g
Processor: S11
Storage: 64GB
Operating system: watchOS 27
Water resistance: 100 metres (10ATM)
Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWB
Sensors: HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeter
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.description:
Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox
From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game
And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure.
As you may have read, this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/Nintendo
Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
When the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I was frankly delighted. My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads.

That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.

articles.description:
Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.
Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.

articles.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
